title: Mathematics for Insurance
text:
The aim of this course is to give you the mathematical tools, and enough distance from them, to bring your existing knowledge to bear on the problems that actually arise in insurance. It is not principally a course in actuarial technique. You will meet pricing formulae, risk measures and copulas, and you will be expected to use them correctly by the end, but the recipes are not the point. What the course tries to offer instead is an account of why insurance contracts take the forms they do, why insurers rely on one class of model rather than another, and where common misconceptions about multivariate risk go wrong.
After a historical introduction, intended to put the field at arm’s length for a moment, the argument runs as follows. A risk-averse agent facing an uncertain loss will pay more than the expected loss to be rid of the risk. An insurer able to pool a large number of such risks can accept them for less than each agent would be willing to pay. That gap is the economic basis of the industry. Everything else — the deductible, the premium loading, portfolio segmentation, reinsurance treaties and solvency capital — comes from working out the details under realistic constraints: asymmetric information, dependent losses, limited capital and regulation.
Working out those details requires a mixture of tools, and assembling that mixture is the real mathematical content of the course.

title: Mathematics for Insurance
text:
The tools we shall need
Decision theory. Expected utility and risk aversion provide the framework in which we analyse the demand for insurance. The analysis of markets under adverse selection and moral hazard explains much of the form that contracts take, and the trade-off between segmentation and pooling.
Optimisation and the calculus of variations. How much is an agent willing to pay to insure a good, or to transfer a risk? Which form of contract is most desirable? We shall meet optimisation problems on the real line, but also problems posed over spaces of functions, which is where the calculus of variations enters. The well-known result on the optimality of the deductible, for instance, is a variational result.
Probability and statistics. Compound distributions, the collective model, heavy tails, dependence structures, and the asymptotic results that justify pooling — together with the circumstances in which those results fail.

title: Mathematics for Insurance
text:
Prerequisites and expectations
You are expected to be comfortable with probability at the level of a first-year master’s course, with standard results in mathematical statistics, and with constrained optimisation. No prior exposure to insurance is assumed beyond what everyday life provides.
Assessment consists of two written examinations, a mid-term examination and a final examination. Mock examinations will be organised, and past exams are available on Moodle.

title: Reading
text: No single book covers the whole course. The list below is deliberately short: each title is particularly useful for one or more chapters, and together they provide a good route through most of the material.

title: Reading
text:
Notes on the list
Denuit and Charpentier is the main reference for Chapters 3 to 6 of the course. Volume I, Principes fondamentaux de théorie du risque, covers premium principles, risk measures, stochastic orderings and dependence; Volume II, Tarification et provisionnement, covers generalised linear models, credibility, bonus–malus systems and reserving. The books are written in French and assume little beyond a solid grounding in probability, making them unusually approachable introductions to a technical literature.
Henriet and Rochet is the main reference for Chapter 2. It is short and precise, covering the supply of and demand for insurance, equilibrium under complete information, and then adverse selection and moral hazard. If you read one book alongside the lectures on contract design, make it this one.
Deelstra and Plantin is a concise volume covering premium calculation principles and the institutional reality of the reinsurance market. It is the English-language complement to Chapters 3 and 5 and is particularly useful because it does not separate the mathematics from the market it describes.
Eeckhoudt, Gollier and Schlesinger is a standard modern treatment of decision-making under risk. Read it for the foundations of Chapter 2, and because it connects insurance with the broader field of financial economics.
Borscheid and Haueter is an edited history of the global insurance industry from the late eighteenth century onwards, with chapters devoted to a wide range of countries. It provides useful background reading for Chapter 1. It is a long book, and you are certainly not expected to read it from cover to cover.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



This introductory chapter is included for general culture and to give historical perspective on the mathematics that follows. It will not be examined: no examination question will require dates, names or historical details from this chapter.
Insurance is much older than the mathematics now used to study it. Communities shared losses, merchants transferred maritime risks and insurers priced uncertain events long before probability had a formal language. The historical order is worth keeping in mind throughout this course: practical problems and institutions usually came first; mathematical models came later.
This is necessarily a selective history. The aim is not to trace every insurance institution, but to follow a few ideas that matter for non-life insurance: solidarity, pooling, risk transfer, information, diversification, reinsurance and the gradual introduction of probability and statistics.
Insurance also has a simple economic interpretation. A contract redistributes money across possible future states: the policyholder pays a certain premium and receives money in some adverse states. In purely monetary terms this transfer does not create wealth by itself, but it can create value for risk-averse agents because money is more useful when a loss has occurred. This is the subject of Chapter 2.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Before probability
Bottomry loans in the ancient Mediterranean, the foenus nauticum, and the gradual separation of the credit element from the risk-transfer element. Genoa and Florence in the fourteenth century provide some of the earliest surviving evidence of recognisably modern marine insurance contracts. The point to emphasise is that functioning insurance markets existed for centuries before anyone could calculate an expected loss: prices were set by custom, bargaining and the underwriter’s judgement of a particular voyage.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: The arrival of the calculus of probability
text:
The arrival of the calculus of probability
Pascal and Fermat; Huygens and the systematic use of mathematical expectation; Halley’s Breslau mortality table of 1693 and his calculation of life-annuity values by age; de Moivre and Annuities upon Lives. The Equitable Life Assurance Society, founded in 1762, was among the early life offices to make systematic use of age-dependent premiums grounded in mortality calculations, helping to establish the professional role from which actuarial science developed.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: The law of large numbers as a business model
text:
The law of large numbers as a business model
Bernoulli, Laplace and the gradual understanding that pooling can turn volatile individual losses into a more predictable aggregate. Lloyd’s and the London market; the expansion of professional reinsurance after the Hamburg fire of 1842, including the creation of Cologne Re in 1846 and Swiss Re in 1863. The emergence of collective risk models and ruin theory in the Scandinavian tradition culminates in the work of Lundberg and Cramér.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Statistics, the state and social insurance
text:
Statistics, the state and social insurance
The Bismarckian social-insurance schemes of the 1880s; the actuarial problems specific to compulsory cover; and the interaction between public provision, mutual institutions and private insurance markets.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Where the mathematics failed
Possible case studies include Equitable Life’s guaranteed-annuity-rate crisis, the underestimation of catastrophe exposure before Hurricane Andrew, and the dependence assumptions embedded in mortgage insurance and monoline guarantees before the global financial crisis. The aim is not to compile a list of scandals, but to develop a working habit: every model in this course has a domain of validity, and the interesting question is always what lies outside it.

title: The demand for insurance
text:
We begin where the economics of insurance begins: with a single agent, facing a single random loss, deciding how much cover to buy. Everything in this part is a consequence of two assumptions — that the agent ranks risky prospects by the expected value of a utility function, and that this function is concave.
The payoff is Mossin’s theorem, which tells us something genuinely surprising. A risk-averse agent offered insurance at a price above its expected cost will never buy full cover, however rich, however cautious, and however small the mark-up. Partial cover is not a compromise forced by budget constraints; it is optimal.

title: The demand for insurance
text:
Preferences over risky prospects
Fix a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). An agent’s final wealth is a random variable \(W\) taking values in an interval \(\mathcal{I} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\). We assume throughout that preferences over such random variables admit an expected-utility representation: there is a function \(u : \mathcal{I} \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(W_1\) is preferred to \(W_2\) exactly when
\[\mathbb{E}[u(W_1)] \geq \mathbb{E}[u(W_2)].\]
The axioms on preferences that deliver this representation — completeness, transitivity, continuity and independence — are due to von Neumann and Morgenstern. We shall take the representation as given and examine its consequences, returning in part 5 to what happens when the independence axiom is dropped.
Two remarks about \(u\). It is determined only up to a positive affine transformation: \(u\) and \(a u + b\) with \(a > 0\) represent the same preferences. And it is a representation of preferences over wealth under risk, not a measure of satisfaction; nothing in what follows requires interpersonal comparison.

Definition 1 (Smooth utility function) A function \(u : \mathcal{I} \to \mathbb{R}\) defined on an open interval \(\mathcal{I}\) is a smooth utility function if

\(u \in \mathcal{C}^2(\mathcal{I})\);
\(u'(w) > 0\) for every \(w \in \mathcal{I}\);
\(u''(w) \leq 0\) for every \(w \in \mathcal{I}\).

Under these assumptions the agent is weakly risk-averse. We shall call the agent strictly risk-averse when \(u'' < 0\) on \(\mathcal{I}\), and risk-neutral when \(u'' \equiv 0\).

Condition (ii) says more is better. Condition (iii) says that the marginal value of an extra euro does not increase as wealth rises. Together with monotonicity, concavity implies — by Jensen’s inequality — that the agent weakly prefers the expected value of any lottery to the lottery itself. Smoothness is a convenience, not a requirement: most of what follows can be proved for concave \(u\) without differentiability, at the cost of working with subgradients.

title: The demand for insurance
section: The certainty equivalent and the risk premium
text:
The certainty equivalent and the risk premium

Definition 2 (Certainty equivalent and risk premium) Let \(u\) be a smooth utility function and let \(W\) be a random variable with values in \(\mathcal{I}\) such that \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\) is finite. The certainty equivalent of \(W\) is the unique \(C(W) \in \mathcal{I}\) satisfying
\[u\bigl(C(W)\bigr) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[u(W)\bigr],\]
and the risk premium attached to \(W\) is
\[\pi(W) = \mathbb{E}[W] - C(W).\]

Existence and uniqueness of \(C(W)\) follow from (ii): \(u\) is a continuous strictly increasing function, hence a bijection onto its range, and \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\) lies in that range. The certainty equivalent is the sure sum the agent regards as exactly as good as the gamble; the risk premium is what they will give up, in expectation, to be rid of the uncertainty.

Proposition 1 (Sign of the risk premium) If \(u\) is a smooth utility function, \(W\) is non-degenerate, \(\mathbb{E}[|W|] < \infty\) and \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\) is finite, then \(\pi(W) \geq 0\), with strict inequality whenever \(u\) is strictly concave.


Proof. By Jensen’s inequality applied to the concave function \(u\), \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)] \leq u(\mathbb{E}[W])\), so \(u(C(W)) \leq u(\mathbb{E}[W])\). Since \(u\) is strictly increasing, \(C(W) \leq \mathbb{E}[W]\), that is \(\pi(W) \geq 0\). If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(W\) is non-degenerate, Jensen’s inequality is strict.

This proposition contains the basic demand-side intuition behind insurance. For a zero-mean risk added to initial wealth, the risk premium is the most the agent would be willing to give up to replace the risky position by a sure one. A risk-neutral counterparty values the same zero-mean risk at zero. The resulting wedge creates room for mutually beneficial risk transfer, before expenses, capital costs and other frictions are introduced.

title: The demand for insurance
text:
The Arrow–Pratt coefficient
The risk premium depends on both the utility function and the risk. We would like a local measure of aversion that depends on \(u\) alone.

Definition 3 (Coefficients of risk aversion) Let \(u\) be a smooth utility function. The coefficient of absolute risk aversion at wealth \(w \in \mathcal{I}\) is
\[A_u(w) = -\frac{u''(w)}{u'(w)},\]
and the coefficient of relative risk aversion is \(R_u(w) = w \, A_u(w)\) for \(w > 0\).

Note that \(A_u\) is invariant under positive affine transformations of \(u\), as it must be if it is to describe preferences rather than a particular representation of them. The curvature \(u''\) alone would not do: it is not invariant, and it has the wrong units.

Proposition 2 (Arrow–Pratt approximation) Let \(u\) be a smooth utility function with \(u \in \mathcal{C}^3\) near \(w \in \mathcal{I}\), and let \(\tilde\varepsilon\) be a bounded random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[\tilde\varepsilon] = 0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\). Write \(\pi(w, k\tilde\varepsilon)\) for the risk premium of the final wealth \(w + k\tilde\varepsilon\). Then, as \(k \to 0\),
\[\pi(w, k\tilde\varepsilon) = \tfrac{1}{2} k^2 \sigma^2 A_u(w) + o(k^2).\]


Proof. Write \(\pi = \pi(w, k\tilde\varepsilon)\), so that by definition \(\mathbb{E}[u(w + k\tilde\varepsilon)] = u(w - \pi)\). Expanding the left-hand side to second order,
\[\mathbb{E}[u(w + k\tilde\varepsilon)] = u(w) + k\,u'(w)\,\mathbb{E}[\tilde\varepsilon] + \tfrac{1}{2}k^2 u''(w)\,\mathbb{E}[\tilde\varepsilon^2] + o(k^2) = u(w) + \tfrac{1}{2}k^2\sigma^2 u''(w) + o(k^2),\]
using \(\mathbb{E}[\tilde\varepsilon] = 0\). Expanding the right-hand side to first order, and noting that \(\pi = O(k^2)\),
\[u(w - \pi) = u(w) - \pi\,u'(w) + o(k^2).\]
Equating the two and dividing by \(u'(w) > 0\) gives \(\pi = -\tfrac{1}{2}k^2\sigma^2 u''(w)/u'(w) + o(k^2)\), which is the claim.

Three things are worth drawing out. The risk premium is, to leading order, proportional to the variance of the risk — which helps explain the role of variance in actuarial practice, and also why variance alone becomes inadequate for large or strongly non-Gaussian risks. The premium is quadratic in the scale \(k\): a zero-mean risk half as large costs approximately a quarter as much to bear. Finally, the two factors separate cleanly: \(\sigma^2\) describes the local scale of the risk, while \(A_u(w)\) describes the agent’s local attitude towards it.

Theorem 1 (Pratt’s comparison theorem) Let \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) be smooth utility functions on \(\mathcal{I}\) with \(u_i'' < 0\). The following are equivalent.

\(A_{u_1}(w) \geq A_{u_2}(w)\) for every \(w \in \mathcal{I}\).
There exists an increasing concave \(\varphi\) with \(u_1 = \varphi \circ u_2\).
\(\pi_1(W) \geq \pi_2(W)\) for every random variable \(W\) with values in \(\mathcal{I}\).


Agent 1 is then said to be more risk-averse than agent 2. The theorem is what licenses the informal use of \(A_u\) as a measure of timidity: a pointwise inequality between two coefficients, which is a local statement about derivatives, turns out to be equivalent to a global statement about every risk the two agents might face. The proof of (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) proceeds by setting \(\varphi = u_1 \circ u_2^{-1}\) and computing \(\varphi''\); we shall do it in the lecture.

Two families
Two parametric families recur throughout the literature, and it is worth knowing why.
Constant absolute risk aversion. Taking \(u(w) = -e^{-aw}\) with \(a > 0\) gives \(A_u \equiv a\). The agent’s willingness to bear a given absolute risk does not depend on their wealth — a strong assumption, and often an unrealistic one, but it makes the demand for insurance independent of initial wealth and so simplifies many calculations. Exponential utility also leads directly to the exponential premium principle; for normally distributed risks, the resulting certainty equivalent reduces to a simple mean–variance expression.
Constant relative risk aversion. Taking \(u(w) = w^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)\) for \(\gamma > 0\), \(\gamma \neq 1\), and \(u(w) = \log w\) for \(\gamma = 1\), gives \(R_u \equiv \gamma\). Here it is the willingness to bear risks proportional to wealth that is constant. Absolute risk aversion \(A_u(w) = \gamma / w\) is decreasing, so this family provides a simple and widely used example of decreasing absolute risk aversion.
The property of decreasing absolute risk aversion, \(A_u' < 0\), is the one most often assumed, and it is the hypothesis under which the comparative statics of the next section behave as intuition suggests.

title: The demand for insurance
text:
The Mossin model
We can now pose the decision problem properly.
An agent with smooth utility \(u\) and initial wealth \(w > 0\) faces a non-degenerate random loss \(X\) with \(0 \leq X \leq w\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \mu > 0\). We assume that all wealth levels appearing below remain in the domain \(\mathcal{I}\) of \(u\). An insurer offers co-insurance: for a fraction \(\alpha \in [0,1]\), the agent is indemnified \(\alpha X\) in exchange for a premium
\[P(\alpha) = (1+\lambda)\,\alpha\mu,\]
where \(\lambda \geq 0\) is the proportional loading. The premium is actuarially fair when \(\lambda = 0\) and carries a mark-up otherwise; the loading pays for the insurer’s expenses, capital and profit.
Final wealth as a function of the chosen cover is
\[W(\alpha) = w - P(\alpha) - X + \alpha X = w - (1+\lambda)\alpha\mu - (1-\alpha)X,\]
and the agent solves
\[\max_{\alpha \in [0,1]} \; V(\alpha), \qquad V(\alpha) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[u(W(\alpha))\bigr].\]

Lemma 1 (Concavity of the objective) \(V\) is concave on \([0,1]\), and strictly concave when \(u'' < 0\) and \(X\) is non-degenerate. Consequently the first-order condition is necessary and sufficient, and the optimum \(\alpha^\ast\) is unique.


Proof. For each fixed realisation of \(X\), the map \(\alpha \mapsto W(\alpha)\) is affine, and \(u\) is concave, so \(\alpha \mapsto u(W(\alpha))\) is concave. Concavity is preserved by taking expectations. If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, then for any \(\alpha_1 \neq \alpha_2\) the random variables \(W(\alpha_1)\) and \(W(\alpha_2)\) differ with positive probability; strict concavity therefore survives after taking expectations.

Differentiating under the expectation, which is justified here because \(X\) is bounded and \(u'\) is continuous,
\[V'(\alpha) = \mathbb{E}\Bigl[u'\bigl(W(\alpha)\bigr)\bigl(X - (1+\lambda)\mu\bigr)\Bigr]. \tag{2.1}\]

Theorem 2 (Mossin’s theorem) Let \(u\) be a smooth utility function with \(u'' < 0\), and let \(\alpha^\ast\) denote the optimal level of cover.

If \(\lambda = 0\), then \(\alpha^\ast = 1\): the agent buys full cover.
If \(\lambda > 0\), then \(\alpha^\ast < 1\): the agent never buys full cover.



Proof. Evaluate (2.1) at \(\alpha = 1\). There \(W(1) = w - (1+\lambda)\mu\) is deterministic, so \(u'(W(1))\) comes out of the expectation:
\[V'(1) = u'\bigl(w - (1+\lambda)\mu\bigr)\,\bigl(\mathbb{E}[X] - (1+\lambda)\mu\bigr) = -\lambda\mu\,u'\bigl(w - (1+\lambda)\mu\bigr).\]
If \(\lambda = 0\) this vanishes. Since \(V\) is concave, \(V'(\alpha) \geq V'(1)=0\) for \(\alpha<1\), so \(V\) is maximised at the upper boundary and \(\alpha^\ast = 1\). If \(\lambda > 0\) then \(V'(1) < 0\) because \(u' > 0\) and \(\mu > 0\), so the optimum must lie strictly below full cover: \(\alpha^\ast < 1\).

The proof is three lines, and the mechanism is worth stating plainly. Near full cover, once the actuarially fair component of the premium is netted out, the benefit from removing the remaining vanishing risk is second-order — by Proposition 2, the value of removing a zero-mean risk of scale \(k\) is of order \(k^2\). The loading, by contrast, creates a first-order marginal cost. A first-order loading cost against a second-order risk-reduction benefit means that the last unit of cover is not worth buying when \(\lambda>0\).
The same argument explains why insurance is bought at all.

Proposition 3 (When cover is bought) Under the assumptions of Theorem 2, \(\alpha^\ast > 0\) if and only if
\[\lambda < \bar\lambda := \frac{\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(u'(w - X),\, X\bigr)}{\mu \; \mathbb{E}\bigl[u'(w - X)\bigr]},\]
and \(\bar\lambda > 0\).


Proof. By Lemma 1, \(\alpha^\ast > 0\) if and only if \(V'(0) > 0\). From (2.1) with \(\alpha = 0\), and \(W(0) = w - X\),
\[V'(0) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[u'(w-X)X\bigr] - (1+\lambda)\mu\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[u'(w-X)\bigr] = \operatorname{Cov}\bigl(u'(w-X), X\bigr) - \lambda\mu\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[u'(w-X)\bigr],\]
which rearranges to the stated condition. For the sign of \(\bar\lambda\): since \(u'' < 0\), the map \(x \mapsto u'(w - x)\) is strictly increasing, so \(u'(w-X)\) and \(X\) are strictly positively correlated whenever \(X\) is non-degenerate, and the covariance is positive.

So there is a threshold loading below which the agent buys positive cover and at or above which they buy none. When \(0 < \lambda < \bar\lambda\), that cover is necessarily partial by Theorem 2; when \(\lambda=0\), full cover is optimal. The covariance in the numerator is the whole story: insurance is valuable because it delivers money precisely in the states where money is most valuable, and \(\bar\lambda\) measures how strong that alignment is.






NoteComparative statics



Three questions to consider before the next session, all answerable from (2.1) by implicit differentiation.
How does \(\alpha^\ast\) respond to an increase in the loading \(\lambda\)? To an increase in initial wealth \(w\), and what does the answer have to do with decreasing absolute risk aversion? And if two agents are ranked by Theorem 1, is the more risk-averse one necessarily the one who buys more cover?

title: The demand for insurance
text:
What comes next
Mossin’s model restricts the contract to a single shape — proportional cover — and asks only how much of it to buy. The natural next question is what happens when the shape is free: among all indemnity schedules \(I(\cdot)\) with a given expected cost, which one does the agent most prefer?
That is a problem of optimisation over a space of functions rather than over a scalar, and the answer, due to Arrow, is the deductible contract. We take it up in the next session, where the calculus of variations does the work that elementary calculus has done here.

title: Outline
text:
The course is organised into six chapters. The first two explore why insurance exists and how insurance contracts are designed. The middle chapters turn to pricing and aggregate-loss modelling, while the final two focus on risk measurement and dependence between risks.


The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
A brief history of insurance, from early forms of risk sharing in Antiquity to the emergence of modern insurance markets. We will discuss the development of marine insurance and the gradual separation of insurance from credit and trade finance in the late Middle Ages; the rise of Lloyd’s; the Great Fire of London and the development of fire insurance; the rationalisation of life insurance; and the emergence of the modern insurance industry. Along the way, we will draw parallels with developments in probability and statistics, from Pascal and Fermat to the law of large numbers and actuarial science, and introduce some of the mathematicians and scientists who played an important part in the history of insurance.
The microeconomics of insurance
Expected utility and risk aversion; the demand for insurance and its dependence on wealth; Mossin’s model; and the optimality of deductible contracts. We conclude with two central problems of insurance markets under asymmetric information: adverse selection and moral hazard.
Pricing, segmentation and the analysis of variance
The individual model and the collective model
Risk measures: Value at Risk, expected shortfall and beyond
Multivariate risks, correlation and copulas

Existence and uniqueness of \(C(W)\) follow from (ii): \(u\) is a continuous strictly increasing function, hence a bijection onto its range, and \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\) lies in that range. The certainty equivalent is the sure sum the agent regards as exactly as good as the gamble; the risk premium is what they will give up, in expectation, to be rid of the uncertainty.

Proposition 1 (Sign of the risk premium) If \(u\) is a smooth utility function, \(W\) is non-degenerate, \(\mathbb{E}[|W|] < \infty\) and \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\) is finite, then \(\pi(W) \geq 0\), with strict inequality whenever \(u\) is strictly concave.


Proof. By Jensen’s inequality applied to the concave function \(u\), \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)] \leq u(\mathbb{E}[W])\), so \(u(C(W)) \leq u(\mathbb{E}[W])\). Since \(u\) is strictly increasing, \(C(W) \leq \mathbb{E}[W]\), that is \(\pi(W) \geq 0\). If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(W\) is non-degenerate, Jensen’s inequality is strict.

This proposition contains the basic demand-side intuition behind insurance. For a zero-mean risk added to initial wealth, the risk premium is the most the agent would be willing to give up to replace the risky position by a sure one. A risk-neutral counterparty values the same zero-mean risk at zero. The resulting wedge creates room for mutually beneficial risk transfer, before expenses, capital costs and other frictions are introduced.

title: The demand for insurance
text:
The Arrow–Pratt coefficient
The risk premium depends on both the utility function and the risk. We would like a local measure of aversion that depends on \(u\) alone.

Definition 3 (Coefficients of risk aversion) Let \(u\) be a smooth utility function. The coefficient of absolute risk aversion at wealth \(w \in \mathcal{I}\) is
\[A_u(w) = -\frac{u''(w)}{u'(w)},\]
and the coefficient of relative risk aversion is \(R_u(w) = w \, A_u(w)\) for \(w > 0\).

Note that \(A_u\) is invariant under positive affine transformations of \(u\), as it must be if it is to describe preferences rather than a particular representation of them. The curvature \(u''\) alone would not do: it is not invariant, and it has the wrong units.

Proposition 2 (Arrow–Pratt approximation) Let \(u\) be a smooth utility function with \(u \in \mathcal{C}^3\) near \(w \in \mathcal{I}\), and let \(\tilde\varepsilon\) be a bounded random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[\tilde\varepsilon] = 0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\). Write \(\pi(w, k\tilde\varepsilon)\) for the risk premium of the final wealth \(w + k\tilde\varepsilon\). Then, as \(k \to 0\),
\[\pi(w, k\tilde\varepsilon) = \tfrac{1}{2} k^2 \sigma^2 A_u(w) + o(k^2).\]


Proof. Write \(\pi = \pi(w, k\tilde\varepsilon)\), so that by definition \(\mathbb{E}[u(w + k\tilde\varepsilon)] = u(w - \pi)\). Expanding the left-hand side to second order,
\[\mathbb{E}[u(w + k\tilde\varepsilon)] = u(w) + k\,u'(w)\,\mathbb{E}[\tilde\varepsilon] + \tfrac{1}{2}k^2 u''(w)\,\mathbb{E}[\tilde\varepsilon^2] + o(k^2) = u(w) + \tfrac{1}{2}k^2\sigma^2 u''(w) + o(k^2),\]
using \(\mathbb{E}[\tilde\varepsilon] = 0\). Expanding the right-hand side to first order, and noting that \(\pi = O(k^2)\),
\[u(w - \pi) = u(w) - \pi\,u'(w) + o(k^2).\]
Equating the two and dividing by \(u'(w) > 0\) gives \(\pi = -\tfrac{1}{2}k^2\sigma^2 u''(w)/u'(w) + o(k^2)\), which is the claim.

Three things are worth drawing out. The risk premium is, to leading order, proportional to the variance of the risk — which helps explain the role of variance in actuarial practice, and also why variance alone becomes inadequate for large or strongly non-Gaussian risks. The premium is quadratic in the scale \(k\): a zero-mean risk half as large costs approximately a quarter as much to bear. Finally, the two factors separate cleanly: \(\sigma^2\) describes the local scale of the risk, while \(A_u(w)\) describes the agent’s local attitude towards it.

Theorem 1 (Pratt’s comparison theorem) Let \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) be smooth utility functions on \(\mathcal{I}\) with \(u_i'' < 0\). The following are equivalent.

\(A_{u_1}(w) \geq A_{u_2}(w)\) for every \(w \in \mathcal{I}\).
There exists an increasing concave \(\varphi\) with \(u_1 = \varphi \circ u_2\).
\(\pi_1(W) \geq \pi_2(W)\) for every random variable \(W\) with values in \(\mathcal{I}\).


Agent 1 is then said to be more risk-averse than agent 2. The theorem is what licenses the informal use of \(A_u\) as a measure of timidity: a pointwise inequality between two coefficients, which is a local statement about derivatives, turns out to be equivalent to a global statement about every risk the two agents might face. The proof of (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) proceeds by setting \(\varphi = u_1 \circ u_2^{-1}\) and computing \(\varphi''\); we shall do it in the lecture.

Two families
Two parametric families recur throughout the literature, and it is worth knowing why.
Constant absolute risk aversion. Taking \(u(w) = -e^{-aw}\) with \(a > 0\) gives \(A_u \equiv a\). The agent’s willingness to bear a given absolute risk does not depend on their wealth — a strong assumption, and often an unrealistic one, but it makes the demand for insurance independent of initial wealth and so simplifies many calculations. Exponential utility also leads directly to the exponential premium principle; for normally distributed risks, the resulting certainty equivalent reduces to a simple mean–variance expression.
Constant relative risk aversion. Taking \(u(w) = w^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)\) for \(\gamma > 0\), \(\gamma \neq 1\), and \(u(w) = \log w\) for \(\gamma = 1\), gives \(R_u \equiv \gamma\). Here it is the willingness to bear risks proportional to wealth that is constant. Absolute risk aversion \(A_u(w) = \gamma / w\) is decreasing, so this family provides a simple and widely used example of decreasing absolute risk aversion.
The property of decreasing absolute risk aversion, \(A_u' < 0\), is the one most often assumed, and it is the hypothesis under which the comparative statics of the next section behave as intuition suggests.

title: The demand for insurance
text:
The Mossin model
We can now pose the decision problem properly.
An agent with smooth utility \(u\) and initial wealth \(w > 0\) faces a non-degenerate random loss \(X\) with \(0 \leq X \leq w\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \mu > 0\). We assume that all wealth levels appearing below remain in the domain \(\mathcal{I}\) of \(u\). An insurer offers co-insurance: for a fraction \(\alpha \in [0,1]\), the agent is indemnified \(\alpha X\) in exchange for a premium
\[P(\alpha) = (1+\lambda)\,\alpha\mu,\]
where \(\lambda \geq 0\) is the proportional loading. The premium is actuarially fair when \(\lambda = 0\) and carries a mark-up otherwise; the loading pays for the insurer’s expenses, capital and profit.
Final wealth as a function of the chosen cover is
\[W(\alpha) = w - P(\alpha) - X + \alpha X = w - (1+\lambda)\alpha\mu - (1-\alpha)X,\]
and the agent solves
\[\max_{\alpha \in [0,1]} \; V(\alpha), \qquad V(\alpha) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[u(W(\alpha))\bigr].\]

Lemma 1 (Concavity of the objective) \(V\) is concave on \([0,1]\), and strictly concave when \(u'' < 0\) and \(X\) is non-degenerate. Consequently the first-order condition is necessary and sufficient, and the optimum \(\alpha^\ast\) is unique.


Proof. For each fixed realisation of \(X\), the map \(\alpha \mapsto W(\alpha)\) is affine, and \(u\) is concave, so \(\alpha \mapsto u(W(\alpha))\) is concave. Concavity is preserved by taking expectations. If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, then for any \(\alpha_1 \neq \alpha_2\) the random variables \(W(\alpha_1)\) and \(W(\alpha_2)\) differ with positive probability; strict concavity therefore survives after taking expectations.

Differentiating under the expectation, which is justified here because \(X\) is bounded and \(u'\) is continuous,
\[V'(\alpha) = \mathbb{E}\Bigl[u'\bigl(W(\alpha)\bigr)\bigl(X - (1+\lambda)\mu\bigr)\Bigr]. \tag{2.1}\]

Theorem 2 (Mossin’s theorem) Let \(u\) be a smooth utility function with \(u'' < 0\), and let \(\alpha^\ast\) denote the optimal level of cover.

If \(\lambda = 0\), then \(\alpha^\ast = 1\): the agent buys full cover.
If \(\lambda > 0\), then \(\alpha^\ast < 1\): the agent never buys full cover.



Proof. Evaluate (2.1) at \(\alpha = 1\). There \(W(1) = w - (1+\lambda)\mu\) is deterministic, so \(u'(W(1))\) comes out of the expectation:
\[V'(1) = u'\bigl(w - (1+\lambda)\mu\bigr)\,\bigl(\mathbb{E}[X] - (1+\lambda)\mu\bigr) = -\lambda\mu\,u'\bigl(w - (1+\lambda)\mu\bigr).\]
If \(\lambda = 0\) this vanishes. Since \(V\) is concave, \(V'(\alpha) \geq V'(1)=0\) for \(\alpha<1\), so \(V\) is maximised at the upper boundary and \(\alpha^\ast = 1\). If \(\lambda > 0\) then \(V'(1) < 0\) because \(u' > 0\) and \(\mu > 0\), so the optimum must lie strictly below full cover: \(\alpha^\ast < 1\).

The proof is three lines, and the mechanism is worth stating plainly. Near full cover, once the actuarially fair component of the premium is netted out, the benefit from removing the remaining vanishing risk is second-order — by Proposition 2, the value of removing a zero-mean risk of scale \(k\) is of order \(k^2\). The loading, by contrast, creates a first-order marginal cost. A first-order loading cost against a second-order risk-reduction benefit means that the last unit of cover is not worth buying when \(\lambda>0\).
The same argument explains why insurance is bought at all.

Proposition 3 (When cover is bought) Under the assumptions of Theorem 2, \(\alpha^\ast > 0\) if and only if
\[\lambda < \bar\lambda := \frac{\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(u'(w - X),\, X\bigr)}{\mu \; \mathbb{E}\bigl[u'(w - X)\bigr]},\]
and \(\bar\lambda > 0\).


Proof. By Lemma 1, \(\alpha^\ast > 0\) if and only if \(V'(0) > 0\). From (2.1) with \(\alpha = 0\), and \(W(0) = w - X\),
\[V'(0) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[u'(w-X)X\bigr] - (1+\lambda)\mu\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[u'(w-X)\bigr] = \operatorname{Cov}\bigl(u'(w-X), X\bigr) - \lambda\mu\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[u'(w-X)\bigr],\]
which rearranges to the stated condition. For the sign of \(\bar\lambda\): since \(u'' < 0\), the map \(x \mapsto u'(w - x)\) is strictly increasing, so \(u'(w-X)\) and \(X\) are strictly positively correlated whenever \(X\) is non-degenerate, and the covariance is positive.

So there is a threshold loading below which the agent buys positive cover and at or above which they buy none. When \(0 < \lambda < \bar\lambda\), that cover is necessarily partial by Theorem 2; when \(\lambda=0\), full cover is optimal. The covariance in the numerator is the whole story: insurance is valuable because it delivers money precisely in the states where money is most valuable, and \(\bar\lambda\) measures how strong that alignment is.






NoteComparative statics



Three questions to consider before the next session, all answerable from (2.1) by implicit differentiation.
How does \(\alpha^\ast\) respond to an increase in the loading \(\lambda\)? To an increase in initial wealth \(w\), and what does the answer have to do with decreasing absolute risk aversion? And if two agents are ranked by Theorem 1, is the more risk-averse one necessarily the one who buys more cover?

title: The demand for insurance
text:
What comes next
Mossin’s model restricts the contract to a single shape — proportional cover — and asks only how much of it to buy. The natural next question is what happens when the shape is free: among all indemnity schedules \(I(\cdot)\) with a given expected cost, which one does the agent most prefer?
That is a problem of optimisation over a space of functions rather than over a scalar, and the answer, due to Arrow, is the deductible contract. We take it up in the next session, where the calculus of variations does the work that elementary calculus has done here.

title: The demand for insurance
text:
Reading for this part
Henriet and Rochet, Microéconomie de l’assurance, chapters 1 and 2. Eeckhoudt, Gollier and Schlesinger, Economic and Financial Decisions under Risk, chapters 1 to 3. Mossin’s original paper, “Aspects of Rational Insurance Purchasing”, Journal of Political Economy 76 (1968), is only a few pages long and is well worth reading directly.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Before money: reciprocity, credit and mutual aid
text:
Before money: reciprocity, credit and mutual aid
A convenient starting point is the observation that exchange does not require coinage. David Graeber’s Debt: The First 5,000 Years famously attacks the textbook story in which isolated individuals first barter, then invent money, and only later discover credit. Drawing on anthropological work, he argues instead that in many small communities people who knew one another relied heavily on reciprocal obligations and informal credit: one household helped another today in the expectation that the favour would eventually be returned (Graeber 2011).
This claim should be stated with care. Graeber did not show that barter never existed, and his broad historical interpretation has itself been debated (Maurer 2013). The more modest point is enough for us: the historical and anthropological record does not support a universal sequence in which societies pass mechanically from barter to money and only then to credit. In communities held together by kinship, neighbourhood, religion or repeated interaction, obligations can be recorded socially rather than settled immediately in cash. Barter certainly occurs, but episodic barter is especially plausible where the parties do not have a durable credit relationship. This is a much weaker – and safer – claim than saying that all exchange among strangers takes the form of barter.
Risk sharing can arise in exactly the same way. A household affected by illness, fire, crop failure or death may receive help from relatives, neighbours, a guild, a village or a religious community. There need be no explicit premium and no calculation of an expected loss. The arrangement is nevertheless recognisably related to insurance: a loss borne by one member of a group is partly absorbed by others. In that sense, informal solidarity is a precursor to formal insurance.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Pooling before insurance: associations in antiquity
text:
Pooling before insurance: associations in antiquity
The ancient Mediterranean world offers more organised examples. Roman voluntary associations (collegia) often combined religious, social and professional functions, and funerary practices were central to many of them (Verboven 2019). Some associations collected entrance fees or regular contributions and used common funds to help provide funerals and burials for deceased members.
It is tempting to describe these organisations simply as “burial insurance”, but that would be too modern a label. Historians have questioned whether there was a distinct legal category of collegia funeraticia. Many associations that financed burials also organised banquets, cultic activity and social life; funeral provision was one function among several (Sakaguchi 2002). What matters here is the economic mechanism: regular contributions to a common fund made an individually lumpy expense collectively more manageable.
That is pooling in a primitive but important sense. It does not yet require probabilities. A group can know from experience that funerals occur regularly without possessing a mathematical model for mortality.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Maritime risk: finance and insurance in the same contract
text:
Maritime risk: finance and insurance in the same contract
Long-distance trade creates a different problem. A merchant who sends a ship across the Mediterranean may lose not only expected profit, but the entire cargo. In antiquity, one response was the maritime loan, often discussed under the Roman terms foenus nauticum or pecunia traiecticia. A lender advanced money for a voyage, but repayment was contingent on safe arrival. If the ship was lost under the conditions specified by the contract, the borrower did not repay the principal (Balard 1978; Piccinno 2016).
The contract therefore bundled two economically distinct services:

financing — the merchant received capital before the voyage;
risk transfer — the lender bore some or all of the maritime loss if the voyage failed.

The lender demanded a high return if the ship arrived safely because that return compensated both for the time value of money and for the possibility of losing the principal. In modern language, the credit spread and the insurance premium were mixed together.
This distinction between financing and risk transfer will become central. A modern insurer does not normally finance the cargo: the merchant may already own it outright. The insurer instead accepts a premium in exchange for taking specified risks. The historical emergence of this separation is one of the decisive steps towards modern insurance.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: The medieval Mediterranean: qirāḍ, muḍāraba, commenda and usury
text:
The medieval Mediterranean: qirāḍ, muḍāraba, commenda and usury
Maritime and long-distance trade flourished across both the Islamic and Christian Mediterranean. In Islamic commercial law, the qirāḍ or muḍāraba was a partnership in which one party supplied capital and another supplied labour and commercial expertise. Profits were shared according to a pre-agreed rule, while financial losses on the invested capital were in principle borne by the capital provider, absent negligence or breach by the agent (Udovitch 1969; Khalilieh 2020).
This is not insurance in the modern sense. It is a way of sharing business risk through the financing contract itself. It is nevertheless highly relevant to our story because it shows that sophisticated risk-sharing institutions existed in the medieval Islamic world without a separate insurance policy.
The prohibition of ribā in Islamic law is often loosely translated as a prohibition of “interest”, but the historical and legal concept is more precise than that. For our purposes, the important point is that a guaranteed increase on a loan was problematic, whereas profit-sharing partnerships such as muḍāraba provided a legitimate way to finance trade while sharing risk. The exact relationship between the Islamic qirāḍ and the European commenda remains a matter of historical debate, but there is substantial scholarship arguing for transmission or influence across the Mediterranean (Khalilieh 2020).
Christian Europe faced its own restrictions on usury. Medieval canon law also made it difficult to charge a simple interest premium for a risky loan. In 1236 Pope Gregory IX’s decretal Naviganti condemned certain gains on maritime loans as usurious. It would be too strong to say that this decree “caused” modern insurance, but religious and legal constraints clearly encouraged merchants and notaries to experiment with contractual forms that separated or disguised financing and risk transfer (Balard 1978).






NoteTwo routes around the same problem



Islamic qirāḍ/muḍāraba and the European commenda kept financing and commercial risk-sharing closely linked: capital was supplied for a venture and the return depended on its success.
The decisive innovation of marine insurance was different: the merchant could finance the venture separately and buy risk transfer as a distinct service.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Fourteenth-century Italy and the birth of modern marine insurance
text:
Fourteenth-century Italy and the birth of modern marine insurance
The strongest surviving evidence for recognisably modern marine insurance comes from the Italian commercial cities of the fourteenth century. Genoa and Florence were especially important, and the practice spread to Palermo, Barcelona, Venice and other Mediterranean centres (Botticini et al. 2023; Leonard 2016).
The central innovation was not simply that somebody bore somebody else’s risk. Maritime loans had done that for centuries. The innovation was that risk could be sold separately from capital.
Suppose a merchant already owns a cargo worth 1,000 florins. Under a maritime loan, the merchant borrows capital and the lender bears the risk of non-repayment if the ship is lost. Under a true insurance arrangement, the merchant may finance the cargo independently and pay, say, a premium of 80 florins to an underwriter who promises to pay a specified indemnity if the insured maritime loss occurs. The risky voyage and the financing of the voyage have become two distinct transactions.

1343, not 1347
Older histories often cite a Genoese contract of 23 October 1347, concerning the ship Santa Clara, as the first pure marine insurance contract. It is a particularly vivid document and remains worth remembering. However, archival work has pushed the surviving evidence earlier. A Genoese document drafted by the notary Tommaso Casanova on 18 March 1343 is now commonly identified as the earliest known modern insurance contract, and another 1343 contract has been found in Palermo involving Genoese and Pisan merchants (Botticini et al. 2023).
The early Genoese contracts were often disguised. The insurer might formally acknowledge a fictitious debt to the insured, supposedly arising from a “free and friendly loan” (gratis et amore), with the debt cancelled if the ship or goods arrived safely. Economically, no genuine loan of the insured amount had been made: the insurer had received a premium and owed the large contractual sum only if the insured loss occurred (Balard 1978). Later contracts also used the legal form of a fictitious sale.
Florentine practice appears to have moved more quickly towards contracts that openly resembled insurance. Whatever the precise legal form, the economic structure was now recognisable: a premium, a defined exposure, named perils or conditions, an insured amount and one or more underwriters.
Two features of modern insurance are already visible:

risk can be divided among several underwriters, so that no single merchant bears the whole loss;
information matters: route, season, vessel, captain, cargo, piracy, war and political conditions all affect the price.

There was still no actuarial expected-loss calculation. Premiums were negotiated from experience, reputation, custom and commercial intelligence. One can think of the underwriter as possessing an implicit subjective probability distribution long before probability had become a mathematical object.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Antwerp, Amsterdam and the institutionalisation of marine insurance
text:
Antwerp, Amsterdam and the institutionalisation of marine insurance
Marine insurance spread north with European trade. Antwerp became an important insurance centre in the sixteenth century; Amsterdam rose to dominance after the commercial shift towards the Dutch Republic. By the end of the sixteenth century, insurance had become important enough in Amsterdam to justify specialised institutions.
In 1598, the city created the Amsterdam Chamber of Insurance and Average (Kamer van Assurantie en Averij), a specialised tribunal for disputes between merchants, insureds, brokers and underwriters (Go 2013). This is a significant institutional step. An insurance market needs more than people willing to take bets on ships: it needs standard practices, enforceable contracts, information, reputation and mechanisms for settling disputes.
The Dutch case also illustrates a broader point. The growth of insurance is tightly connected to the growth of commerce. As ships travel farther and capital committed to a single voyage grows larger, the value of transferring and spreading maritime risk also grows.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Lloyd’s: a market built around information
text:
Lloyd’s: a market built around information
The most famous example of this relationship between information and underwriting is Lloyd’s of London.
Edward Lloyd operated a coffee house in the City of London in the late seventeenth century. Coffee houses were not merely places to drink coffee: different establishments attracted particular commercial and professional communities. Lloyd’s became associated with merchants, shipowners, captains and others interested in shipping intelligence. The first surviving public reference to the coffee house dates from 1688 (Lloyd’s 2026b).
The essential economic asset of the coffee house was information. Who had sailed? Which vessel had arrived? Which captain was reliable? Where were privateers operating? What was the condition of a ship? In a world without instant communication, better shipping news was itself a form of risk-management technology.
Underwriters could subscribe portions of a marine risk rather than one person taking the entire exposure. A broker or merchant would circulate the proposed risk; different underwriters would write their names beneath it and state the share they were prepared to accept. This is the origin of the word underwriting in its insurance sense.
Lloyd’s moved to Lombard Street in 1691. Lloyd’s List, providing shipping intelligence, began under that name in 1734. A more formal subscription market emerged during the eighteenth century, and in 1771 a group of subscribers created what became “New Lloyd’s” (Lloyd’s 2026a). Lloyd’s was therefore not originally an insurance company with one balance sheet. It was, and remains in a transformed form, a market in which separate risk-bearing entities underwrite business under common rules and infrastructure.

Insurance, global trade and slavery
The economic argument for insurance is powerful: by reducing the financial consequences of loss, it can make long-distance trade and investment feasible. But an institution that facilitates trade does not distinguish morally between good and bad trade.
British marine insurance, including the Lloyd’s market, became deeply entangled with the Atlantic slave economy. Insurance was written on slave ships and on enslaved people treated in law and commerce as cargo; more broadly, insurers covered the shipping and plantation economy built around slavery (Pearson and Richardson 2019; Draper 2026). This is not a marginal footnote. It is a reminder that a technology can be economically efficient while serving profoundly unethical ends.
The right conclusion is therefore not that insurance is inherently good or bad. It is that risk-transfer technology expands the set of activities that can be financed and undertaken. The social value of that expansion depends on the activity itself.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Fire insurance after the Great Fire of London
text:
Fire insurance after the Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London began on 2 September 1666 and destroyed more than 13,000 houses together with major civic and religious buildings (London Fire Brigade 2026b). The event made the concentration of urban fire risk painfully visible.
Commercial fire insurance developed rapidly afterwards. Nicholas Barbon established the Fire Office in 1680, and several competing fire insurers followed (London Fire Brigade 2026a). Policyholders displayed metal fire marks on insured buildings. These identified the insurer, advertised the company and, in a city before systematic street numbering, helped locate insured properties.
Insurers also employed firefighting teams. The popular story that a company’s brigade would simply stand aside while an uninsured or rival-insured building burned is misleading. There is little evidence for such a general practice; insurers had an obvious incentive to stop fires from spreading, and reciprocal arrangements between companies developed (London Museum 2026).
Fire insurance therefore combined three ideas that remain central today:

pooling: many property owners pay premiums, while only some suffer fires;
risk prevention: the insurer has an incentive to reduce the probability and severity of loss;
information and classification: construction, location and use of a building affect the premium.

The Industrial Revolution would make these issues much larger. A fire in a workshop is one thing; a fire in a large textile mill full of machinery, workers and inventories is another.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Life insurance, mortality tables and the birth of actuarial pricing
text:
Life insurance, mortality tables and the birth of actuarial pricing
Life insurance deserves a place in this history even though the remainder of this course is concerned with non-life insurance. It was in life insurance and annuities that mathematical pricing first became systematic.
Life-contingent contracts existed before modern actuarial science. The Amicable Society for a Perpetual Assurance Office, founded in London in 1706, is a useful example of the transitional stage. It organised long-term life assurance through a mutual pool, but initially charged members essentially uniform contributions within the eligible age range rather than calculating an individual premium from age-specific mortality. The benefit itself also depended on the resources available for distribution. In other words, one could operate a life-assurance institution before possessing a modern actuarial pricing system (Ogborn 1962).
The crucial development was the construction of credible mortality tables and the combination of mortality with compound interest.
John Graunt’s Natural and Political Observations … upon the Bills of Mortality of 1662 is a landmark in demography and contains an early attempt to infer a life table from London mortality data (Graunt 1662; Sutherland 2005). In 1693, Edmond Halley used data from Breslau (now Wrocław) to construct a much more systematic mortality table and explicitly used it to calculate the value of life annuities at different ages (Halley 1693).
Abraham de Moivre developed the mathematics of life annuities further in Annuities upon Lives (1725), using a simplified law of mortality that made calculations tractable. James Dodson later argued for level premiums that depended on age at entry. Although he died before the institution opened, his work helped lead to the foundation in 1762 of the Society for Equitable Assurances on Lives and Survivorships, commonly known as the Equitable. The Equitable became famous for long-term contracts with premiums systematically differentiated by age and type of assurance, and for the increasing role of mathematical expertise in life assurance (Ogborn 1962; Society of Actuaries 2026). Richard Price subsequently played an important role in its actuarial calculations, and William Morgan, appointed actuary in 1775, helped turn regular valuation of liabilities and surplus into institutional practice.
This sequence is fundamental:

life insurance existed before actuarial science, but mortality data and probability made it possible to replace crude rules with systematic age-dependent valuation.







NoteAnd the tontine?



A tontine is related to this story, but it is better viewed as a life-contingent financing and annuity arrangement than as ordinary indemnity insurance. Lorenzo Tonti proposed his famous scheme to the French government in 1653. Participants contributed capital; the income allocated to a group was redistributed among the survivors as members died. Tontines therefore pool longevity risk, and historically they helped connect public finance, annuities and the mathematics of survival (Hellwege 2018).
They are interesting here because they show, once again, that institutional experimentation with uncertain lifetimes preceded accurate actuarial valuation.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Insurance and industrialisation
During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, insurance became part of the infrastructure of industrial capitalism. Factories, warehouses, railways, ships and urban property represented increasingly large concentrations of capital. Insurance did not “cause” the Industrial Revolution, but it made some investments easier to finance and some losses easier to absorb. Fire insurers also accumulated large datasets on buildings and industrial hazards and increasingly differentiated risks by construction, occupancy and process (Pearson 2004).
Insurance companies simultaneously became important institutional investors. Premiums are collected before many claims are paid, especially in long-duration life business. Insurers therefore hold and invest substantial pools of capital. British life assurance companies, for example, became major participants in capital markets during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries (Bogle et al. 2022).
The range of insurable objects also widened. Marine and fire insurance were joined by accident, employers’ liability, engineering and machinery cover, railway risks and, later, motor, aviation and many forms of professional and product liability. The twentieth and twenty-first centuries extended the same logic to ever more specialised exposures, from natural catastrophes to cyber risk. This proliferation is a recurring feature of insurance history: new technologies create wealth and opportunities, but also new loss mechanisms for which households and firms seek protection (Borscheid and Haueter 2012).
Industrialisation also exposed the limits of primary insurance. A single urban catastrophe could damage thousands of insured properties at once. The problem was no longer merely to pool independent household losses; it was to survive accumulation risk.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Reinsurance: insurance for insurers
Reinsurance is a natural response to concentration. A primary insurer cedes part of its portfolio to another risk bearer, thereby limiting its exposure to individual policies, events or entire portfolios.
Large nineteenth-century fires accelerated the development of professional reinsurance. The Hamburg fire of 1842 produced very large losses for an increasingly international insurance market. Cologne Re, founded in 1846, is generally regarded as the first independent professional reinsurer. Swiss Re was founded in 1863 in a period when industrialisation and urban concentration were creating demand for additional risk-bearing capacity; the Glarus fire of 1861 highlighted the problem, although historians caution against treating that fire as the sole cause of the company’s creation (Borscheid et al. 2013; Swiss Re 2026).
Reinsurance adds another level of pooling:

households and firms pool through insurers;
insurers pool and diversify further through reinsurers;
global reinsurance spreads catastrophe risk across countries and capital providers.

This layered structure is still central to non-life insurance today.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Social insurance, compulsory insurance and the state

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
From judgement to probability
The history above contains an apparent paradox. Marine insurance markets were functioning in the fourteenth century, but the mathematical theory of probability did not begin to take recognisable form until the seventeenth century.
How could insurers price risk without probability?
The answer is that one can make probabilistic judgements without a calculus of probability. Medieval and early-modern underwriters knew that some routes were more dangerous than others, that winter sailing could be more hazardous, that war increased losses, that some captains and ships had better reputations, and that diversification across voyages reduced the chance of complete ruin. Their “probabilities” were implicit and subjective, embedded in market prices and judgement rather than written as numbers satisfying axioms.

Pascal, Fermat and Huygens
The conventional starting date for mathematical probability is 1654, when Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat corresponded about problems of games of chance, especially the fair division of stakes in an interrupted game. These were not insurance problems. They were gambling problems, but they forced mathematicians to reason systematically about uncertain future outcomes.
Christiaan Huygens published De ratiociniis in ludo aleae in 1657, the first printed treatise devoted to probability. The language was still that of games and “expectation”, but a general principle was emerging: uncertain payoffs could be compared by weighting outcomes according to their chances.
This mathematical idea would eventually become the fair-premium benchmark
[ = [X], ]
where (X) is a random loss. Real insurance premiums must of course include expenses, capital costs, risk margins and market considerations, but expected loss is the conceptual starting point.


Bernoulli and the law of large numbers
Jacob Bernoulli’s Ars Conjectandi, published posthumously in 1713, contains the first rigorous form of what we now call the law of large numbers (Mattmüller 2014). In modern notation, for independent identically distributed losses (X_1,X_2,) with finite mean,
[ _{i=1}^n X_i [X_1]. ]
For insurance, the economic interpretation is immediate: under suitable conditions, the average loss in a large pool is more stable than an individual loss.
But one should not reverse the historical causality. Insurers had been pooling risks for centuries before Bernoulli proved the theorem. The law of large numbers did not invent pooling; it explained mathematically why pooling can work.
And the hypotheses matter. If losses are strongly dependent, adding more policies does not diversify aggregate risk nearly as effectively. A hurricane can damage thousands of houses simultaneously. A financial crisis can generate many liability claims at once. The mathematical question is therefore not simply “How many policies do we have?” but “What is the dependence structure?”


From de Moivre to the central limit theorem
Abraham de Moivre’s work of 1733 gave a normal approximation to the binomial distribution. Laplace later generalised the asymptotic argument, with a major formulation appearing in his Théorie analytique des probabilités of 1812 (Hald 1990). These results are ancestors of the central limit theorem.
In modern notation, under familiar conditions,
[ N(0,1). ]
For insurers, this offers much more than convergence of averages. It gives an approximation to the distribution of aggregate fluctuations around the mean, and therefore to quantiles, capital requirements and safety margins.
Again, the historical development of the theorem was not driven primarily by insurance. Probability theory was growing out of gambling, astronomy, error theory, demography and pure mathematics. Insurance became one important field of application.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Modern probability came later still
Even the probability theory of Laplace was not yet modern probability in the measure-theoretic sense used in this course.
At the turn of the twentieth century, Émile Borel and Henri Lebesgue developed ideas of measure and integration that made it possible to handle infinite sets of outcomes rigorously. In his work on denumerable probabilities in 1909, Borel introduced ideas closely connected with almost-sure convergence and obtained an early form of the strong law of large numbers for binary expansions (Cléry and Mazliak 2022). The modern general theorem came only through later work by Cantelli, Khinchin, Kolmogorov and others.
The decisive axiomatic synthesis came with Andrei Kolmogorov’s Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung in 1933. Kolmogorov defined probability as a measure on a measurable space and placed conditional probability, expectation, independence and stochastic processes in a common framework (Kolmogorov 1933; Plato 2005).
This is worth emphasising because it corrects another possible historical misconception:

modern probability was not invented by insurers in order to price insurance.

Insurance problems contributed to the demand for quantitative risk methods, especially in life contingencies and later risk theory, but the modern mathematical foundations of probability were part of a much broader development in analysis and measure theory.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: The Scandinavian turn: from probability to non-life risk theory
text:
The Scandinavian turn: from probability to non-life risk theory
The connection with non-life insurance becomes much more direct in the work of the Scandinavian actuarial school.
In 1903, the Swedish actuary Filip Lundberg modelled the surplus of an insurance company as a stochastic process and studied the probability of ruin. Harald Cramér later put Lundberg’s ideas on firmer mathematical foundations and developed what became known as collective risk theory (Cramér 1969; International Actuarial Association 2026).
A stylised version of the classical model is
[ U_t = u + ct - _{k=1}^{N_t}Y_k, ]
where

(u) is the insurer’s initial capital,
(c) is the premium income rate,
(N_t) is a claim-counting process,
(Y_k) are claim sizes.

The central question is no longer merely “What is the expected loss?” but
[ P!(_{t} U_t < 0), ]
that is, the probability that the insurer is eventually ruined.
This is recognisably the beginning of modern non-life actuarial mathematics: claim counts, claim severities, aggregate losses, dependence, reserves, solvency and reinsurance are treated as stochastic objects rather than as rules of thumb.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: What to retain for the rest of the course
text:
What to retain for the rest of the course
There are five broad lessons from this history.
First, insurance does not begin with probability. Risk transfer and pooling can function through custom, repeated interaction and market judgement.
Second, a decisive institutional innovation is the separation of financing from insurance. Once risk itself can be priced and traded independently, insurance becomes a distinct industry.
Third, pooling is not magic. Its effectiveness depends on the number of risks, their heterogeneity, their tails and, crucially, their dependence. This will reappear throughout the course.
Fourth, insurance is inseparable from information and incentives. Medieval merchants, Lloyd’s underwriters and modern actuaries all face versions of the same questions: what does the insured know, what does the insurer know, how can risk be classified, and how does insurance change behaviour?
Finally, modern insurance is a layered risk-sharing system. Policyholders transfer risk to insurers; insurers transfer risk to reinsurers and capital markets; states regulate the system and sometimes absorb risks that private markets cannot or will not bear. The mathematics becomes progressively more sophisticated, but the underlying economic problem remains surprisingly stable.
